name: Maximalism

influenced_by: a direct, stated reaction against 2010s minimalism

reacts_against: the Marie Kondo-driven decluttering and minimalism movement that dominated interior-design and lifestyle media through the 2010s, arguing explicitly that density and personal history, not emptiness, make a space feel alive.
article: Maximalism as a named design-media trend gained real traction from around 2017 on, explicitly and repeatedly framed by design journalists as the direct opposite of the minimalism (and specifically the Marie Kondo-driven decluttering movement) that had dominated the previous decade's home and lifestyle coverage. Rather than naming one specific visual style, maximalism functions as an umbrella position — more pattern, more color, more collected objects, more personal history visible in a room — under which several more specific aesthetics (cluttercore, grandmillennial) sit as particular flavors. The maximalism-versus-minimalism framing has repeated itself across design history before (the Memphis Group's 1980s embrace of pattern and color was itself a reaction against mid-century modernism's restraint), which design historians have noted as a recurring pendulum swing rather than a one-time 2010s event.

findings: mostly muted — about 44% of the measured color is low-saturation (greys, dusty tones)
measured.caveat: Colors measured from Aesthetics Wiki images as photographed and displayed on screen; actual materials vary, and screen colors are approximate.
